exam: How would you use local birth and death rates to prioritize a new vaccination programme? — Identify age groups with highest mortality, choose vaccines that address leading causes (e.g., measles, hepatitis B).

A district reports a sudden rise in under‑5 mortality. What immediate steps should you take? — Verify data accuracy, assess for outbreaks (e.g., diarrhoea, malaria), initiate emergency treatment kits, and notify public‑health authorities.

Distinguish between demography and epidemiology when answering a case‑based question. — Explain demography describes population structure; epidemiology describes disease patterns within that structure.
What demographic indicator would you monitor to evaluate the impact of a new antiretroviral clinic? — Track adult HIV prevalence and age‑specific mortality trends over 12‑months.
In a refugee camp, which demographic data guide your triage of acute illnesses? — Age distribution, proportion of children <5, and prevalence of chronic conditions (e.g., TB, HIV).
Why might crude death rates be misleading in a rural setting? — Under‑reporting of home deaths and migration out of the area can artificially lower the rate.
How does rapid urban migration affect the burden of non‑communicable diseases? — Increases sedentary lifestyle and dietary changes, raising hypertension and diabetes prevalence among young adults.
When faced with missing laboratory capacity, how can you still assess population health trends? — Rely on clinical syndromic surveillance, verbal autopsies, and sentinel site reporting.
ai.title: Population Health Demography
ai.subject: Public health
ai.summary: Demography studies size, structure, and changes of human populations. Clinicians use demographic data to anticipate disease patterns, allocate resources, and tailor interventions in low‑resource settings.

b: Key metrics: crude birth rate, crude death rate, infant mortality rate, total fertility rate, life expectancy.
sections.p: Demography quantifies births, deaths, migration, and age‑sex composition of a community. In clinical practice it is inferred from census, health‑facility registers, and verbal autopsy data.

b: Stage I: low mortality, high life expectancy (>70 years).
Stage II: moderate mortality, life expectancy 55‑70 years.
Stage III: high mortality, life expectancy <55 years.
sections.p: Population health is graded by mortality and morbidity indices. High‑mortality settings (e.g., under‑5 mortality > 80/1,000) signal severe demographic stress.

b: Infectious diseases: HIV, TB, malaria, hepatitis B.
Maternal‑child factors: obstetric complications, malnutrition.
Non‑communicable rise: hypertension, diabetes, cancers.
Migration: rural‑to‑urban drift, refugee influx.
sections.p: Determinants of demographic change in East Africa include infectious disease burden, maternal health, nutrition, and migration patterns.

b: High under‑5 mortality → frequent severe diarrhoea, pneumonia.
Young adult HIV prevalence → opportunistic infections.
Aging rural populations → rising stroke and heart failure.
sections.p: Clinicians see demographic effects as clusters of disease, age‑specific presentation patterns, and resource gaps.
Population data are gathered through surveys, facility registers, and simple calculations.

t.b: What is the current fertility and mortality profile? – Gives crude birth/death rates, informs service planning.
What caused deaths where no medical record exists? – Provides cause‑specific mortality fractions for policy.
What are trends in institutional deliveries and in‑hospital mortality? – Highlights gaps in care quality.
Use community health worker reports and sentinel site data – Gives approximate rates for urgent decision‑making.

b: Sudden rise in infant mortality > 80/1,000.
Sharp increase in HIV prevalence > 5 % in adults.
Mass displacement without health‑service linkage.
sections.p: Rapid demographic shifts can overwhelm health systems, leading to outbreaks and service collapse.

Community‑based HIV testing and antiretroviral rollout in high‑prevalence zones.
Nutrition programmes for under‑5 children in areas with low birth weight prevalence.
Strengthen referral pathways for chronic NCDs as life expectancy rises.
sections.p: Clinicians act on demographic signals by prioritising preventive and curative interventions aligned with the most pressing population needs.

Update DHS‑type surveys every 5 years.
Integrate demographic dashboards into district health information systems.
sections.p: Continuous monitoring of demographic indicators guides resource allocation and evaluates impact of interventions.

b: Epidemiology focuses on disease incidence; demography on births, deaths, migration.
sections.p: Demography is sometimes mixed up with epidemiology, but the former describes population structure while the latter studies disease distribution.

sections.p: Incomplete registration can underestimate mortality, especially in remote areas.
